title: First Internship Application Kit
subtitle: The three things to check before you submit, plus the message to send after — none of which require pretending you have experience you do not have.
fromVideo: From the video: before your first internship application
intro: The application puts your name in the pile. A project and a good conversation give them something to remember. Work through the checklist, then send the message. Nothing here asks you to invent a title or a job you did not have.

entries.title: Your resume names a project, not just classes
entries.lead: Open your resume. Find one line that is a thing you finished, not a course you took.
items: If it is there, make sure it has a verb, a result, and a link or a number.
If it is not there, you are not ready to submit yet. Pick one project and finish it first.
Do not write "intern" for something that was not an internship. Write "project" and say what you did.
entries.note: Classes show you attended. A project shows you finished something without being graded on it.

action.label: Get the project starter
action.note: If this step stopped you, start there — it walks you through picking and finishing one project.

entries.title: Your LinkedIn headline says what you are building toward
entries.lead: Go beyond your school name. Someone reading it should know what you are into in under three seconds.
items: Weak: "Student at [High School]" — true, but it says nothing.
Better: what you are building toward plus where you are. Example: "High school student building skills in marketing and analytics."
Keep it honest. Do not claim a role, a company, or a title you do not hold.

action.label: Get the resume starter
action.note: An editable one-page template with the project section already laid out.

entries.title: After you apply, find one person and ask a specific question
entries.lead: Pick one person and ask one question, without asking for a referral.
items: Do not open by asking for a referral, a job, or an internship. That ends the conversation before it starts.
Ask about their work. Example: "What skill mattered most when you started in this role?"
Keep it to three or four lines. Say who you are, say you applied, ask the one question, stop.
entries.note: You are starting a conversation, not submitting a second application.

entries.title: The follow-up
entries.lead: What to do with the answer, and when to let it go.
items: If they reply, thank them and say what you did with the answer. "I looked into the tool you mentioned and built X with it" is the strongest second message you can send.
If they do not reply within a week, leave it. One message, no chasing. People are busy and it is not about you.
Either way, write down the tool, skill, or problem they mentioned and go learn it.

rule.title: Before you hit submit
items: One project line on the resume, with a verb, a result, and a link or number.
A LinkedIn headline that says what you are building toward.
One person found, one specific question written and sent.
Nothing on the application you could not explain out loud.

verifyNote: The example wording here is an example, not a script to paste. Put it in your own words before you send it.
